# Data Acquisition, Cleaning & Preparation

(Tasks 1-3)

```{r}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
#Task 1: Data Acquisition
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 7, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event)
}

# Task 2: Fix Column Titles
NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()

NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  rename(
    title = Title,
    runtime = Runtime,
    views = Views,
    hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
    release_date = `Release Date`,
    available_globally = `Available Globally?`
  )

#Task 3: Fix Column Types
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year),
    available_globally = available_globally == "Yes"
  )

```

## Task 5: Exploratory Questions - Inline Values

**Question 1: What date range is covered by this data set?**

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    earliest_period = min(period_start),
    latest_period = max(period_end)
  )
```
The date range  covered by this data set is **January 1, 2023 (2023-01-01) to July 30, 2026 (2026-07-30)**.



**Question 2: How many different shows and movies are covered in this data set?**

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    distinct_titles = n_distinct(title)
  )
```
There are **24,427** different shows and movies covered in this data set. 



**Question 3: How many total hours have been spent watching shows from the *Bridgerton* universe?**

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours_viewed_bridgerton = sum(hours_viewed)
  )
```
A total of **4,862,800,000** hours have been spent watching shows from the *Bridgerton* universe. 



**Question 4: How many total hours have been spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things?**

```{r}
# For this question, we only want the “real” *Stranger Things* shows and not the companion behind-the-scenes show (“Beyond Stranger Things”), the animated spin-off (“Tales from ’85”), or the background music (“Stranger Things: Fireplace”).

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Fireplace")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Tales From")) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )
```

A total of **5,548,500,000** hours have been spent watching the five seasons of *Stranger Things* excluding the BTS, spin-off and background music.



**Question 5: What percentage of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1?**

> Step 1: Calculate total watch time in 2026H1
```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  summarise(
    total_2026h1_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )
```

> Step 2: Identify the Top 10 titles based on total views in 2026 H1
```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    total_views = sum(views, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_views)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

> Step 3: Calculate total hours viewed for the Top 10 titles

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  filter(title %in% c(
    "His & Hers: Limited Series",
    "Bridgerton: Season 4",
    "I Will Find You: Limited Series",
    "Stranger Things 5",
    "Run Away: Limited Series",
    "Teach You a Lesson: Limited Series",
    "ONE PIECE: Season 2",
    "Man on Fire: Season 1",
    "Ms. Rachel: Season 1",
    "The Night Agent: Season 3"
  )) |>
  summarise(
    top_10_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )

```

> Final step is the calculation: top_10_hours_viewed / total_2026h1_hours_viewed * 100 = (4138400000 / 74333600000) * 100) =  5.57%

The Top 10 titles accounted for **`r sprintf("%.2f%%", (4138400000 / 74333600000) * 100)`** of total viewing time.



**Question 6: What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available? (Answer this both by title and weighted by hours viewed)**

> Part 1: Calculate Netflix’s catalog globally available by title

```{r}
# Step 1: Calculate Netflix’s total available titles (we already calculated this in Q2)

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    distinct_titles = n_distinct(title)
  )

# Step 2: Calculate Netflix’s total globally available titles
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(available_globally == TRUE) |>
  summarise(
    titles_available_globally = n_distinct(title, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

```

> Final step is calculation: Fraction of Netflix’s globally available catalog by hours viewed is globally_available_hours_viewed / total_hours_viewed * 100 = (265637100000 / 511590500000) * 100) = 24.60%


> Part 2: Calculate Netflix’s catalog globally available weighted by hours viewed

```{r}
# Step 1: Calculate Netflix’s total hours viewed
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    total_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )

# Step 2: Calculate total hours viewed for titles available globally

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(available_globally == TRUE) |>
  summarise(
    globally_available_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )

```

> Final step is calculation: Fraction of Netflix’s globally available catalog by hours viewed is globally_available_hours_viewed / total_hours_viewed * 100 = (265637100000 / 511590500000) * 100) = 51.92%

Fraction of Netflix’s globally available catalog by title is **`r sprintf("%.2f%%", (6010 / 24427) * 100)`** and weighted by hours viewed is **`r sprintf("%.2f%%", (265637100000 / 511590500000) * 100)`**



## Task 6: Exploratory Questions - Table Answers

**Question 1: What was the top show (by total hours viewed) in each period and what fraction of total viewership did it capture?**  

**Approach**: To analyze the top shows across each period by *"total hours viewed"*, first, I calculated total viewing hours by title and period. Then, I divided each top show's volume by total platform viewership, and used slice_max() to extract only the top show in each period. 

```{r}

library(dplyr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Computing the top show and its share per period
top_shows_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>

  # Aggregating hours viewed by period and title, in case titles appear multiple times in a period
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(
    hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), 
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Grouping by period only to calculate the period total and fraction
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(
    period_total = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    fraction = hours_viewed / period_total
  ) |>
  # Isolating the row with the maximum hours viewed for each period
  slice_max(order_by = hours_viewed, n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

# Step 2: formatting using gt
top_shows_by_period |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, fraction) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = hours_viewed,
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = fraction,
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = md("**Reporting Period**"),
    title = md("**Top Show**"),
    hours_viewed = md("**Total Hours Viewed**"),
    fraction = md("**Fraction of Viewership**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Table 1: Top Netflix Show by Period**"),
    subtitle = md("*Peak Viewership Analysis*")
  )

```

**Wednesday: Season 2 ** was the *top performing show in 2025H2*, attracting **964.1 million hours** viewed and capturing **1.35% of total viewership**. The result suggests that Wednesday: Season 2 had the strongest relative performance compared with other titles in its reporting period. Additionally, it has the highest viewership share among all the top shows across the seven reporting periods.  



**Question 2: How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions? You should consider both the number of titles and the total runtime of content.**  

**Approach**: To answer this question, I grouped the data by reporting period and ordered it chronologically using period_start so I could accurately track change in both number of distinct catalogs and total runtime over time. Counting distinct titles prevents duplicate entries from skewing the numbers and adding total runtime reveals the growth in volume growth. 

```{r}
# Step 1: Summarizing catalog size by period
catalog_evolution <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, period_start) |>  # including period_start to keep data chronologically sorted
  summarise(
    total_titles = n_distinct(title),
    total_runtime = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(period_start) # Sorting chronologically

# Step 2: creating table using gt
catalog_evolution |>
  select(period, total_titles, total_runtime) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_titles, total_runtime),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = md("**Period**"),
    total_titles = md("**Number of Titles**"),
    total_runtime = md("**Total Runtime**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Table 2: Evolution of Netflix Catalog Size**"),
    subtitle = md("*Tracking Title Count and Total Runtime Across Reporting Periods*")
  )
```

Netflix had the highest number of titles but the lowest total runtime in the first half of 2023. In the second half of the year, the number of titles dropped significantly, while total runtime increased. In the following periods, both the number of titles and total runtime gradually increased. This pattern suggests that Netflix’s catalog became smaller but potentially generated greater viewership in the second half of 2023. The increase in runtime despite having fewer titles may also indicate a shift toward longer content or titles that attracted more viewing. 



**Question 3: Which shows have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods?**

**Approach**: This Question, made me approach the answer in several ways but I ultimately chose this version because I felt it gave me the most accurate answer. 

To identify consistently high-performing shows across all periods, I grouped titles by franchise, combining individual seasons and volumes into a single universe. I then calculated each franchise’s number of periods present in, mean, minimum, maximum, and standard deviation of hours viewed across periods.

To focus on franchises with consistently high viewership, I ranked them by highest average hours viewed, while filtering presence in at least five periods and setting minimum hours viewed to of 300 million and maximum hours viewed to 700 million hours. These criteria helped me to reduce the influence of one-time hits and identify franchises that maintained high viewership over time and are true "staples". 

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Cleaning show titles and aggregate performance across periods
staples_high_floor <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    show_name = str_replace(
      title, 
      regex("([:\\s\\-]+)?(season|volume|part|limited series).*$", ignore_case = TRUE), 
      ""
    ),
    show_name = str_trim(show_name)
  ) |>
  group_by(show_name, period) |>
  summarise(
    period_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop_last"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    periods_present = n_distinct(period),
    mean_hours = mean(period_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_hours = min(period_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_hours = max(period_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_hours = sd(period_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Step 2: Filtering for presence across 5+ periods with minimum and maximum hours 
  filter(
    periods_present >= 5,
    max_hours >= 700000000,
    min_hours >= 300000000	
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_hours)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

# Step 3: create table using gt
staples_high_floor |>
  select(show_name, periods_present, min_hours, mean_hours, max_hours, sd_hours) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(min_hours, mean_hours, max_hours, sd_hours),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    show_name = md("**Show**"),
    periods_present = md("**Periods Active**"),
    min_hours = md("**Min Hours**"),
    mean_hours = md("**Mean Hours**"),
    max_hours = md("**Max Hours**"),
    sd_hours = md("**Std. Deviation**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Table 3: Best Performing Franchises by Viewership**"),
    subtitle = md("*Performance Ranked by Highest Average Hours Viewed with a Presence Across 5+*")
  )
```
The shows have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods based on this approach are **Suits (2011), Grey's Anatomy, Gilmore Girls** and **The Walking Dead**.  



**Question 4: Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?**  

**Approach**: To answer this question, I classified content as either TV Shows or Movies using a combination of title keywords (like season, limited series, volume, part) and a runtime threshold of more than 240 minutes (4 hours). Then, I calculated the total viewing hours for each content type across reporting periods and converted them into percentage shares. This helped me to distinguish between longer films and TV series, making it easier to compare their share of total viewership over time. 

``` {r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Creating the content type
classified_netflix <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    # Classifying as TV Show or Movie based on title text and runtime
    content_type = case_when(
      str_detect(title, regex("season|limited series|volume|part", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "TV Show",
      runtime > 240 ~ "TV Show", # Anything over 4 hours total runtime is a show
      TRUE ~ "Movie"             # Defaulting everything else to Movie
    )
  )

# Step 2: Aggregating hours viewed by period and content type
period_content_split <- classified_netflix |>
  group_by(period, period_start, content_type) |>
  summarise(
    hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Calculating the fraction of total viewership for each content type for each period
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(
    period_total = sum(hours_viewed),
    fraction = hours_viewed / period_total
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(period_start)

# Step 3: Formatting using gt and using pivot wider for clean comparison table
period_content_split |>
  select(period, content_type, fraction) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = content_type,
    values_from = fraction
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(`TV Show`, Movie),
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = md("**Reporting Period**"),
    `TV Show` = md("**TV Shows (%)**"),
    Movie = md("**Movies (%)**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Table 4: Viewership Share of TV Shows vs Movies**"),
    subtitle = md("*Viewership Share Based on Runtime Across Reporting Periods*")
  )
```
Within each period, the fraction of time spent on shows is significantly higher than movies. The time spent on movies in the first half of 2023, although, still lower than shows was relatively higher than the time spent on movies in rest of the time periods. However, this number noticeably dropped for the rest of the time periods. This indicates that shows dominated viewership by a huge margin throughout all given time periods.  



**Question 5: How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?**

**Approach**: For this question, I divided the catalog into live events and pre-taped content and calculated summary statistics for each category, including title counts, means, medians, 90th percentiles, and maximum viewing hours. Comparing both viewership and top-performing titles helped me understand how the two categories performed withough being skewed by outliers. 

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Cleaning dataset 
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  # 1. Detecting and removing aggregate placeholders to get accurate metrics
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(
    # 2. Deriving live_event boolean using standard pipeline regex
    live_event = str_detect(
      title, 
      regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ) & !str_detect(
      title, 
      regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  )

# Step 2: Summarizing viewership metrics comparing live events vs. pre-taped content
live_comparison <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  group_by(live_event) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles = n(),
    mean_hours   = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_hours = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90_hours    = quantile(hours_viewed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE), # this is top tier
    max_hours    = max(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),           # hit
    .groups      = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(live_event, "Live Events", "Pre-Taped Content")
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_titles))

# Step 3: create table using gt
live_comparison |>
  select(content_type, total_titles, mean_hours, median_hours, p90_hours, max_hours) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_titles, mean_hours, median_hours, p90_hours, max_hours),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    content_type = md("**Content Type**"),
    total_titles = md("**Total Count**"),
    mean_hours   = md("**Average Hours Viewed**"),
    median_hours = md("**Median Hours Viewed**"),
    p90_hours    = md("**Top Tier (90th Percentile)**"),
    max_hours    = md("**Maximum (Peak Hit)**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Table 5: Live Events vs Pre-Taped Content Performance**"),
    subtitle = md("*Comparing Average and Top-Tier Viewership*")
  ) 

```


Pre-taped content averaged *8.2 Million* viewing hours, whereas Live events average *5.2 Million* hours, indicating that Pre-taped content outperformed live events in both average viewing hours and the 90th-percentile or top-tier threshold. This suggests that pre-taped content benefits from longer viewing windows, allowing titles to accumulate views over time.


> I wanted to dive a little deeper to compare the viewership against the catalog shares. Considering that live events have a very small catalog share, pre-taped content is at an advantage: 

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Cleaning dataset and classifying under live_event
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  # 1. Filtering aggregate/summary placeholders
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(
    # 2. Classifying live events vs pre-taped using regex logic
    live_event = str_detect(
      title, 
      regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ) & !str_detect(
      title, 
      regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  )

# Step 2: creating platform baselines
total_platform_titles <- nrow(cleaned_netflix_data)
total_platform_hours  <- sum(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Summarizin metrics by content type
live_efficiency_summary <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  group_by(live_event) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles     = n(),
    catalog_share    = n() / total_platform_titles,
    total_hours      = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    viewership_share = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE) / total_platform_hours,
    
    yield_per_title  = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 
    efficiency_index = (sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE) / total_platform_hours) / (n() / total_platform_titles),
    
    # creating distribution benchmarks
    median_hours     = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90_hours        = quantile(hours_viewed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_hours        = max(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(live_event, "Live Events", "Pre-Taped Catalog")
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(catalog_share))

# Step 4: rendering gt table
live_efficiency_gt <- live_efficiency_summary |>
  select(
    content_type, total_titles, catalog_share, total_hours, viewership_share, 
    efficiency_index, median_hours, p90_hours, max_hours
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_titles, total_hours, median_hours, p90_hours, max_hours),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(catalog_share, viewership_share),
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(efficiency_index),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    content_type     = md("**Content Type**"),
    total_titles     = md("**Catalog Count**"),
    catalog_share    = md("**Catalog Share (%)**"),
    total_hours      = md("**Total Viewership Hours**"),
    viewership_share = md("**Viewership Share (%)**"),
    efficiency_index = md("**Efficiency Index**"),
    median_hours     = md("**Median Hours**"),
    p90_hours        = md("**Top Tier (90th Pctl)**"),
    max_hours        = md("**Peak Hit**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Table 6: Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content Efficiency**"),
    subtitle = md("*Evaluating Catalog Share, Total Viewership, and Efficiency Index*")
  )

# display table
live_efficiency_gt
```

Live events accounted for just *0.3%* of the catalog (190 titles) but generated over 1 billion viewing hours, representing *0.2%* of total platform viewing hours. Their Efficiency Index of *0.64*, compared with *1.00* for pre-taped content, indicates lower viewing efficiency relative to the platform benchmark. However, live events can still attract substantial audiences, with peak viewing hours exceeding *235 Million* despite their small share of the catalog.




# Final Deliverable: Platform Strategy Memo

## Strategy Memo

**To**: Netflix Leadership  
**From**: Naaz Parvaz  
**Date**: 16th October, 2026  
**Subject**: Corporate Strategy Memo


## Purpose
This memorandum evaluates the performance of Netflix’s pre-taped, long-form content, including movies and TV Shows, across global and regional categories from the first half of 2023 through the first half of 2026 (2023H1–2026H1). The analysis aims to inform Netflix’s 2027 content strategy by identifying portfolio inefficiencies, guiding investment decisions such as production and licensing, and providing a data-driven approach to manage catalog quality and size.


## Background
Pre-taped content represents *99.7%* of Netflix’s catalog, making its performance central to effective resource allocation. For this analysis, content is divided into four categories: Global TV Shows, Regional TV Shows, Global Movies, and Regional Movies. Each category is evaluated against platform-wide engagement benchmarks, with titles performing below the 25th percentile (>P25) classified as **under-performing**.


## Key Findings

**1. Movies account for most under-performing titles:**  
Although movies (combined Global and Regional) represent *29.2%* of the catalog, they account for nearly *84%* of **under-performing** titles. This imbalance suggests that movie acquisition and retention practices need to be investigated more closely.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true

library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Clean dataset, filter out live specials, & define segments
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  # 1. Remove aggregate placeholders
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  # 2. Filter out Live / Event Specials to sync with Pre-Taped Catalog
  filter(
    !(
      str_detect(title, regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)) & 
      !str_detect(title, regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE))
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex(
          "season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", 
          ignore_case = TRUE
        )
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

# Step 2: Establish total platform catalog count and percentile thresholds
clean_total_titles <- nrow(cleaned_netflix_data)

p90_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE)
p75_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
p25_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Summarise performance per segment with BOTH Total Titles and Catalog Share
hit_rate_summary <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles     = n(),
    catalog_share    = n() / clean_total_titles,
    top_tier_pct     = mean(hours_viewed >= p90_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    strong_pct       = mean(hours_viewed >= p75_clean & hours_viewed < p90_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    moderate_pct     = mean(hours_viewed >= p25_clean & hours_viewed < p75_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    underperform_pct = mean(hours_viewed < p25_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Standardize row order
  mutate(
    segment = factor(
      segment, 
      levels = c("Global TV Shows", "Regional TV Shows", "Global Movies", "Regional Movies")
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(segment)

# Step 4: Render GT Table
exec_hit_rate_matrix <- hit_rate_summary |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_titles), 
    use_seps = TRUE, 
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(catalog_share, top_tier_pct, strong_pct, moderate_pct, underperform_pct), 
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    segment          = md("**Segment**"),
    total_titles     = md("**Total Titles**"),
    catalog_share    = md("**Catalog Share**"),
    top_tier_pct     = md("**Top Hits (>=P90)**"),
    strong_pct       = md("**Strong (P75–P90)**"),
    moderate_pct     = md("**Moderate (P25–P75)**"),
    underperform_pct = md("**Underperforming (<P25)**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Table 7: Netflix Portfolio Performance (Pre-Taped Catalog)**"),
    subtitle = md("*Share of Titles and Performance Distribution Across Strategic Quadrants*")
  )

# Display Table
exec_hit_rate_matrix
```

**2. Regional Movies present the greatest efficiency concern:**  
Regional Movies account for *23.6%* of the catalog, yet *53.2%* of titles in this category are observed to be **under-performing**. Historical data also show that under-performance declined when the category’s title count dropped sharply from *9,599 to 460* in the second half of 2023 (2023H2), then increased as titles were added to the catalog again in the first half of 2024 (2024H1). This pattern suggests that expanding the regional movie catalog without selective acquisition criteria may increase the volume of low-engagement and under-performing content. The chart below represents the positive correlation between catalog size and under-performance.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Step 1: Cleaning data
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  filter(
    !(
      str_detect(title, regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)) & 
      !str_detect(title, regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE))
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex("season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

# Step 2: Establishing underperformance benchmark
p25_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Aggregating period metrics and filtering for Regional Movies
correlation_data_reg_movies <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  mutate(period = if_else(is.na(period), "Unspecified", as.character(period))) |>
  group_by(period, segment) |>

    total_titles     = n(),
    underperform_pct = mean(hours_viewed < p25_clean, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,

  filter(segment == "Regional Movies")

r_val_rm   <- cor(correlation_data_reg_movies$total_titles, correlation_data_reg_movies$underperform_pct, use = "complete.obs")
```

**3. Format of content impacts its performance:**  
Regional TV Shows account for *41.3%* of the catalog and perform in line with their catalog share, with an Efficiency Index of *1.00* and an under-performance rate of *14.8%*. In contrast, Regional Movies represent *23.6%* of the catalog but have a substantially higher under-performance rate of *53.2%*. This suggests that regional content is not inherently less effective. Instead, its performance significantly varies by format.

## Recommendations

**1. Remove under performing content and license selectively:**  
Reduce regional movie licensing by removing titles that have consistently under-performed. (*Consider contractual obligations before removal*) Adopt a more selective approach to regional movie licensing and prioritize films with stronger audience appeal and clearer evidence of demand. This would maintaining a regional reach while directing more resources toward content categories that have demonstrated consistent performance.

**2. Prioritize successful content format:**
Prioritize successful content format like Regional TV Shows over Regional Movies and by maintaining investment in proven regional series and identifying opportunities to expand further within that.

**3. Reallocate Resources toward high-performing content:**  
Redirect resources from under-performing movie licenses toward high-performing Global TV Shows and Regional TV Shows. Evaluate investments by comparing performance to to catalog share, acquisition or production costs and long-term audience value.  


## Conclusion
Netflix’s 2027 content strategy should prioritize catalog performance and engagement efficiency over catalog expansion alone. The concentration of under-performing titles in movie categories, particularly Regional Movies, highlights an opportunity to improve acquisition decisions and reduce unnecessary licensing costs. A well-defined approach to catalog curation, combined with targeted investment in stronger-performing TV Shows, can help Netflix allocate resources more effectively while maintaining a diverse and strategically valuable content for their audience.

**1. Platform Composition:**  

> To begin my analysis, I wanted to start by understanding Netflix's platform composition. This meant the catalog and viewership share of pre-taped vs. live events.



```{r}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Cleaning data 
classified_netflix <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  # 1. Filter out aggregate placeholders
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  # 2. Filtering out Live Events
  filter(
    !(
      str_detect(title, regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)) & 
      !str_detect(title, regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE))
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # 3. creating format classification
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex("season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    # 4. creating availability classification 
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    # Construct 4 quadrants
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

# Step 2: Aggregating title counts by period and segment
period_title_counts <- classified_netflix |>
  # Replace NA periods with "Unspecified" if any exist so no rows are dropped
  mutate(period = if_else(is.na(period), "Unspecified", as.character(period))) |>
  group_by(period, segment) |>
  summarise(
    title_count = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Step 3: using pivot wider and creating gt table
period_title_counts |>
  select(period, segment, title_count) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = segment,
    values_from = title_count,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>

  select(
    period, 
    `Global TV Shows`, 
    `Regional TV Shows`, 
    `Global Movies`, 
    `Regional Movies`
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(`Global TV Shows`, `Regional TV Shows`, `Global Movies`, `Regional Movies`),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = md("**Reporting Period**"),
    `Global TV Shows` = md("**Global TV Shows**"),
    `Regional TV Shows` = md("**Regional TV Shows**"),
    `Global Movies` = md("**Global Movies**"),
    `Regional Movies` = md("**Regional Movies**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Table 9: Title Count by Segment Across Reporting Periods**"),
    subtitle = md("*Synchronized Catalog Volume Across Global vs. Regional Quadrants*")
  )
```

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Clean data
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  # 1. Remove aggregate placeholders
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  # 2. Filter out Live / Event Specials so totals match the Pre-Taped Catalog subset
  filter(
    !(
      str_detect(title, regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)) & 
      !str_detect(title, regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE))
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex(
          "season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", 
          ignore_case = TRUE
        )
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

clean_total_titles <- nrow(cleaned_netflix_data)
clean_total_hours  <- sum(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 2: Summarise Portfolio Matrix Data
portfolio_matrix_data <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles     = n(),
    catalog_share    = n() / clean_total_titles,
    viewership_share = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE) / clean_total_hours,
    efficiency_index = viewership_share / catalog_share,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Set custom row order and sort
  mutate(
    segment = factor(
      segment, 
      levels = c("Global TV Shows", "Regional TV Shows", "Global Movies", "Regional Movies")
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(segment)

# Step 3: GT Table
exec_portfolio_matrix <- portfolio_matrix_data |>

  fmt_number(columns = c(total_titles), use_seps = TRUE, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(catalog_share, viewership_share), decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(efficiency_index), decimals = 2) |>
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Clean dataset, filter out live specials, & define segments
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  # 1. Remove aggregate placeholders
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  # 2. Filter out Live / Event Specials to sync with Pre-Taped Catalog
  filter(
    !(
      str_detect(title, regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)) & 
      !str_detect(title, regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE))
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex(
          "season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", 
          ignore_case = TRUE
        )
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

# Step 2: Establish total platform catalog count and percentile thresholds
clean_total_titles <- nrow(cleaned_netflix_data)

p90_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE)
p75_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
p25_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Summarise performance per segment with BOTH Total Titles and Catalog Share
hit_rate_summary <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles     = n(),
    catalog_share    = n() / clean_total_titles,
    top_tier_pct     = mean(hours_viewed >= p90_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    strong_pct       = mean(hours_viewed >= p75_clean & hours_viewed < p90_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    moderate_pct     = mean(hours_viewed >= p25_clean & hours_viewed < p75_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    underperform_pct = mean(hours_viewed < p25_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Standardize row order
  mutate(
    segment = factor(
      segment, 
      levels = c("Global TV Shows", "Regional TV Shows", "Global Movies", "Regional Movies")
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(segment)

# Step 4: Render GT Table
exec_hit_rate_matrix <- hit_rate_summary |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_titles), 
    use_seps = TRUE, 
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(catalog_share, top_tier_pct, strong_pct, moderate_pct, underperform_pct), 
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    segment          = md("**Segment**"),
    total_titles     = md("**Total Titles**"),
    catalog_share    = md("**Catalog Share**"),
    top_tier_pct     = md("**Top Hits (>=P90)**"),
    strong_pct       = md("**Strong (P75–P90)**"),
    moderate_pct     = md("**Moderate (P25–P75)**"),
    underperform_pct = md("**Underperforming (<P25)**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Table 7(used above in memo): Netflix Portfolio Performance (Pre-Taped Catalog)**"),
    subtitle = md("*Share of Titles and Performance Distribution Across Strategic Quadrants*")
  )

# Display Table
exec_hit_rate_matrix
```
  
**4. Netflix Portfolio Performance:**  

> This table gives a quick overview of the Performance by each segment. The reason this is more efficient is that instead of basing this analysis simply on averages, which could be skewed due to outliers, chunking viewership by percentile tiers helped me unmask performance correctly across the catalog.   
  

```{r}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: CLean Data
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  # 1. Remove aggregate placeholders
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  # 2. Filter out Live / Event Specials
  filter(
    !(
      str_detect(title, regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)) & 
      !str_detect(title, regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE))
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex("season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

# Step 2: Calculate Platform-Wide P25 Benchmark
p25_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Summarize Total Titles vs Underperforming Titles for each Segment
underperformance_summary <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles          = n(),
    underperforming_titles = sum(hours_viewed < p25_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    segment = factor(
      segment, 
      levels = c("Global TV Shows", "Regional TV Shows", "Global Movies", "Regional Movies")
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(segment)

# Step 4: Render Clean GT Table
underperformance_summary |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_titles, underperforming_titles),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    segment                = md("**Segment**"),
    total_titles           = md("**Total Titles**"),
    underperforming_titles = md("**Underperforming Titles (< P25)**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Table 11: Under-performance by Segment (Pre-Taped Catalog)**"),
    subtitle = md("*Total Catalog Size vs Number of Under-performing Titles*")
  )
```

**5. Underperformance by Segement:**  

> This table focuses only on the Under-performance of each segement, presenting the under-performance against number of titles. 
  

```{r}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Clean data
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  filter(
    !(
      str_detect(title, regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)) & 
      !str_detect(title, regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE))
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex("season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

# Step 2: Create platform-wide percentile benchmarks
p90_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE)
p75_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
p25_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Render GT tables
create_segment_period_gt <- function(df, target_segment) {
  df |>
    filter(segment == target_segment) |>
    mutate(period = if_else(is.na(period), "Unspecified", as.character(period))) |>
    group_by(period) |>
    summarise(
      total_titles     = n(),
      top_tier_pct     = mean(hours_viewed >= p90_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
      strong_pct       = mean(hours_viewed >= p75_clean & hours_viewed < p90_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
      moderate_pct     = mean(hours_viewed >= p25_clean & hours_viewed < p75_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
      underperform_pct = mean(hours_viewed < p25_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups          = "drop"
    ) |>
    gt() |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(total_titles), use_seps = TRUE, decimals = 0) |>
    fmt_percent(columns = c(top_tier_pct, strong_pct, moderate_pct, underperform_pct), decimals = 1) |>
    cols_label(
      period           = md("**Reporting Period**"),
      total_titles     = md("**Total Titles**"),
      top_tier_pct     = md("**Top Hits (>=P90)**"),
      strong_pct       = md("**Strong (P75–P90)**"),
      moderate_pct     = md("**Moderate (P25–P75)**"),
      underperform_pct = md("**Underperforming (<P25)**")
    ) |>
    tab_header(
      title    = md(paste0("**Table 12: ", target_segment, "- Performance Tier Distribution Across Reporting Periods**")),
      subtitle = md("*Tracking Hit Density and Long-Tail Under-performance Over Time*")
    ) 
}

# Step 4: Create the 4 individual GT tables
gt_global_tv_shows   <- create_segment_period_gt(cleaned_netflix_data, "Global TV Shows")
gt_regional_tv_shows <- create_segment_period_gt(cleaned_netflix_data, "Regional TV Shows")
gt_global_movies     <- create_segment_period_gt(cleaned_netflix_data, "Global Movies")
gt_regional_movies   <- create_segment_period_gt(cleaned_netflix_data, "Regional Movies")

# Step 5: Render all 4 in the chunk output so it is easy (for me) to switch between them in RStudio
gt_global_tv_shows
gt_regional_tv_shows
gt_global_movies
gt_regional_movies
```
**6. Performance Distribution by Each Segment:**  

> This section spotlights each of the four individual performance distribution tables for each segment over all seven time periods. The goal here is to track long-tail performance over time. The performance is broken down into top hits, strong performance, moderate performance and under-performance. This allowed me to see the impact that the change in catalog size had on the performance for each segment and led me to conclude that the increase in catalog size led to an increase in under-performance fo regional and global movie segments. 


```{r}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpmisc) # Required for stat_poly_eq() and stat_poly_line()
library(scales)

# Step 1: Clean data and classify into 4 strategic quadrants
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  filter(
    !(
      str_detect(title, regex("live at|live from|live stream|comedy special|stand-up|special event|vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE)) & 
      !str_detect(title, regex("you vs\\.|lopez vs\\.|snack vs\\.|ash vs\\.|godzilla vs\\.|scott pilgrim vs\\.|vampires vs\\.", ignore_case = TRUE))
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex("season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

# Step 2: Establish platform-wide P25 benchmark
p25_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Aggregate period-by-period metrics for correlation analysis
correlation_data <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  mutate(period = if_else(is.na(period), "Unspecified", as.character(period))) |>
  group_by(period, segment) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles     = n(),
    underperform_pct = mean(hours_viewed < p25_clean, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, # as percentage
    .groups          = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    segment = factor(
      segment, 
      levels = c("Global TV Shows", "Regional TV Shows", "Global Movies", "Regional Movies")
    )
  )

# Step 4: Create ggplot with regression line and R-squared annotation
ggplot(correlation_data, aes(x = total_titles, y = underperform_pct, color = segment)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_poly_line(se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  stat_poly_eq() +
  facet_wrap(~segment, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  scale_color_brewer(type = "qual", palette = 2, name = "Segment") +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 6: Correlation of Catalog Size and Underperformance Rate",
    subtitle = "Evaluating Long-Tail Inefficiency Across Segments",
    x = "Total Catalog Size (Title Count)",
    y = "Underperformance Rate (< P25)"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(face = "italic", size = 11, hjust = 0.5, color = "gray30"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#e8e8e8", color = "gray50"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```
